--- title: "Precision–recall curves" description: "Evaluating the flagged cases when positives are rare: PR curves, average precision, precision and lift in the top k%, and the role of the base rate." --- **Question answered:** of the cases the model flags, how many are real positives, and how many of the real positives does it find? ## Why look beyond ROC The [ROC curve](roc-auc.qmd) measures false alarms *relative to all negatives*: the false positive rate is FP / (FP + TN). With 96\.3% of policies without a claim, that denominator is huge, and a small false positive rate can hide a large number of false alarms: At a threshold of 0.1, the GBM has a false positive rate of only 3\.3%: a point far to the left on the ROC curve. But that is 5\,412 false alarms against 1\,180 correctly flagged claims, so only 18% of the flagged policies actually have a claim. **Precision** relates false alarms to true hits instead of to all negatives, so it shows directly what happens among the flagged cases. That makes it the natural metric when positives are rare and attention goes to the cases the model flags: fraud checks, claim reviews, medical screening, marketing campaigns. ## The precision–recall curve The PR curve uses the same threshold sweep as the ROC curve, but plots - **recall** (true positive rate: the share of all claims we flag) on the x-axis, against - **precision** (the share of flagged policies with a claim) on the y-axis. Starting from a very high threshold, only the highest-risk policies are flagged: recall is small and, for a good model, precision is high. Lowering the threshold raises recall and, usually, lowers precision, until everything is flagged: recall 1 and precision equal to the overall claim rate. ::: {#cell-fig-pr .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = plot_pr(y, {m: b[m] for m in models}, ylim=0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Precision–recall curves on the test set. Thin gray curves connect points with the same F1 score.](precision-recall_files/figure-html/fig-pr-output-1.png){#fig-pr width=557 height=420} ::: ::: Three things differ from a ROC plot: - **The baseline is the claim rate, not a diagonal.** Flagging at random gives a precision equal to the claim rate (3\.7%) at every recall. - **The curve isn't monotone.** Precision can go up *or* down when the threshold drops, so the curve is jagged, especially on the left where few policies are flagged and each one changes precision noticeably. - **The left part matters most.** It shows the highest-risk policies, which is where a review or intervention would start. Here the GBM clearly beats the GLM, even though their ROC curves were close. The gray curves connect points of equal **F1 score**, the harmonic mean of precision and recall. The best F1 the GBM reaches is 0\.185 (at threshold 0\.10), against 0\.153 for the GLM. Low values like these are typical for rare events. F1 is only a convenient summary: it weights precision and recall equally, which rarely matches the actual costs of misses and false alarms. ## Average precision **Average precision** (AP) condenses the PR curve into one number: the precision at each threshold, weighted by how much recall that threshold adds, $$ \text{AP} = \sum_k (R_k - R_{k-1})\, P_k, $$ where $R_k$ and $P_k$ are recall and precision after lowering the threshold past the $k$-th distinct score. The Null model's AP equals the claim rate. Using the same ten toy policies as on the ROC page: ::: {#tbl-toy-pr .cell tbl-cap='Precision and recall of the ten toy policies, and each threshold\'s contribution to AP.' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} toy_y = np.array([1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0]) toy_p = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.55, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]) toy = pr_points(toy_y, toy_p) toy["AP contribution"] = np.diff(np.r_[0, toy["recall"]]) * toy["precision"] toy.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

The AP is 0\.830: on average, when the threshold passes a policy with a claim, 83% of the flagged policies have a claim. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Don't use the trapezoidal area Computing the area under the PR curve with the trapezoidal rule (as for ROC) connects the points with straight lines. Between two PR points, precision does not change linearly, so the result is off, in either direction, and it also depends on which starting point is assumed at recall 0. On the toy example it gives 0\.811 instead of 0\.830. With many distinct scores the gap shrinks, but AP is the well-defined summary: `average_precision_score` in scikit-learn, whereas `sklearn.metrics.auc` on a PR curve is the trapezoidal version. ::: ## ROC and PR tell different stories ::: {#tbl-auc-ap .cell tbl-cap='Ranking metrics of both models. \'AP / claim rate\' shows how many times better than random the average precision is.' execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame({ "AUC": auc, "Average precision": ap, "AP / claim rate": {m: ap[m] / rate for m in models}, }).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
AUC Average precision AP / claim rate
GLM 0.694 0.093 2.534
GBM 0.713 0.116 3.152
``` ::: ::: The GBM's AUC is 0\.018 higher than the GLM's, a modest 3%. Its average precision is 24% higher. Both metrics summarize the same ranking, but they weight it differently: - **AUC** weighs all pairs of a claim and a non-claim equally, wherever they are in the ranking. - **AP** weighs the top of the ranking most: a claim ranked first raises precision at every later threshold. The GBM's advantage is concentrated in its highest-risk predictions, so AP shows it more clearly. ## Precision and lift in the top k% In practice, capacity is often fixed: 'we can review 5% of policies'. Then the relevant question is how good the top 5% of the ranking is. Two measures answer it: - **precision at k%**: the share of flagged policies with a claim, and - **lift at k%**: precision divided by the overall claim rate, i.e. how many times more claims the flagged group contains than a random group of the same size. ::: {#tbl-top-k .cell tbl-cap='Flagging the k% of policies with the highest predicted probability.' execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} shares = [0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20] top = pd.concat( {m: pd.DataFrame({f"top {s:.0%}": top_share_metrics(y, b[m], s) for s in shares}).T for m in models}, axis=1, ) top.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
GLM GBM

``` ::: ::: Flagging the top 1%, the GBM finds 7\.7 times more claims than random selection would, the GLM 5\.6 times. As the flagged share grows, precision falls towards the claim rate and lift towards 1. Showing lift for every decile of the ranking gives a **lift chart**, the subject of a later page. ## Precision depends on the claim rate Precision has a property that matters a lot in practice: unlike the ROC curve, it **depends on the base rate**. At any threshold, $$ \text{precision} = \frac{\pi \cdot \text{TPR}}{\pi \cdot \text{TPR} + (1 - \pi) \cdot \text{FPR}}, $$ where $\pi$ is the share of positives. TPR and FPR are properties of the model alone. Precision mixes them with $\pi$. To see the effect, we keep all policies with a claim and randomly drop policies without a claim until the claim rate reaches 10%, 20% and 50%. The model and its ranking don't change. ::: {#58201631 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} rng = np.random.default_rng(0) pos, neg = np.flatnonzero(y == 1), np.flatnonzero(y == 0) samples = {} for target in (rate, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50): n_neg = min(len(neg), int(len(pos) * (1 - target) / target)) idx = np.r_[pos, rng.choice(neg, n_neg, replace=False)] samples[f"{target:.1%}"] = (y.to_numpy()[idx], b["GBM"].to_numpy()[idx]) ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-prevalence .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} ramp = ["#86b6ef", "#3987e5", "#1c5cab", "#0d366b"] # light to dark: rising claim rate fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.6)) axes[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color=MUTED, linewidth=1) for (label, (ys, ps)), color in zip(samples.items(), ramp): roc, pr = roc_points(ys, ps), pr_points(ys, ps) axes[0].plot(roc["fpr"], roc["tpr"], color=color, label=f"claim rate {label} (AUC {auc_rank(ys, ps):.3f})") axes[1].plot(np.r_[0, pr["recall"]], np.r_[pr["precision"].iloc[0], pr["precision"]], drawstyle="steps-pre", color=color, label=f"claim rate {label} (AP {average_precision(ys, ps):.3f})") axes[0].set(xlabel="False positive rate", ylabel="True positive rate", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1.01), aspect="equal") axes[1].set(xlabel="Recall", ylabel="Precision", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1.01)) axes[0].legend(loc="lower right") axes[1].legend(loc="upper right") fig.tight_layout() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The same GBM evaluated at different claim rates (by subsampling policies without a claim). Left: ROC curves. Right: precision–recall curves.](precision-recall_files/figure-html/fig-prevalence-output-1.png){#fig-prevalence width=1066 height=494} ::: ::: The ROC curves lie on top of each other: AUC doesn't change. The PR curves rise with the claim rate, and AP climbs from 0\.12 to 0\.71. **Same model, same ranking, different AP.** This has practical consequences: - **Don't compare AP across datasets, segments or time periods with different base rates.** A higher AP may only mean more positives. Report the base rate next to every AP, or report AP / base rate. - **Balanced test sets inflate precision.** Undersampling negatives, common in fraud and medical studies, makes precision look far better than it will be in production. - **Precision drifts when the base rate drifts.** If the claim rate drops next year, the precision of the same model at the same threshold drops too, even though nothing about the model has changed. This is one reason to monitor the base rate along with model metrics. ## ROC or PR? The two curves contain the same information (given the base rate, every ROC point maps to exactly one PR point), but they emphasize different things: | | ROC / AUC | PR / AP | |---|---|---| | Focus | the whole ranking, both classes | the top of the ranking, positive class | | False alarms measured relative to | all negatives | true hits | | Depends on base rate | no | yes | | Random baseline | 0.5 | base rate | | Good for | comparing rankings across populations; when both error types matter | rare positives where only the flagged cases are acted on | It's often claimed that AP is 'the right metric for imbalanced data'. That's too simple. Imbalance alone doesn't make AUC wrong. Recent work (McDermott et al., 2024) shows that AP favors improvements at the top of the ranking and can favor models that work best for the subgroups with the highest base rates. **Choose by the question**: use AUC when the whole ranking matters, AP or precision at k% when only the top of the ranking is acted on, and report the base rate with any precision-based metric. ## Takeaways - **Precision** relates false alarms to true hits, which is what matters when positives are rare and only flagged cases are acted on. - The **PR curve**'s baseline is the base rate. **Average precision** is its correct summary; don't use the trapezoidal area. - AP weights the **top of the ranking**. Here it shows the GBM's advantage (24%) much more clearly than AUC (3%). - With fixed capacity, report **precision and lift at k%**. - Precision and AP **depend on the base rate**. Never compare them across populations with different base rates, and watch them change when the base rate drifts.
